title: When Funding Becomes Leverage, Trust Becomes the Real Asset
excerptForBlog:
Elon Musk, September 20, 2017: "Either go do something on your own or continue with OpenAI as a nonprofit. I will no longer fund OpenAI until you have made a firm commitment to stay or I'm just being a fool who is essentially providing free funding for you to create a startup. Discussions are over."

Ilya Sutskever, in the same thread: "The current structure provides you with a path where you end up with unilateral absolute control over the AGI. You stated that you don't want to control the final AGI, but during this negotiation, you've shown to us that absolute control is extremely important to you… Thus, we are concerned that as the company makes genuine progress towards AGI, you will choose to retain your absolute control of the company despite current intent to the contrary… The goal of OpenAI is to make the future good and to avoid an AGI dictatorship. You are concerned that Demis could create an AGI dictatorship. So do we. So it is a bad idea to create a structure where you could become a dictator if you chose to, especially given that we can create some other structure that avoids this possibility."

screenshots.caption: Source document — Musk v. Altman (OpenAI) — Exhibit 15 · Musk v. Altman (OpenAI) · 4:24-cv-04722 (CAND), Doc. 353-19, filed 2025-11-07

lessonTitle: When Funding Becomes Leverage, Trust Becomes the Real Asset
pullQuote: The moment your funder's leverage looks like a path to absolute control, your co-founders stop building and start negotiating their exit.
situation: On September 20, 2017, Elon Musk sent an ultimatum to OpenAI's leadership: commit fully or lose his funding. Ilya Sutskever replied in the same thread, pointing out a structural contradiction — the governance path being negotiated would give Musk 'unilateral absolute control over the AGI,' even as Musk stated he did not want that control. The tension is not just personal. It is a live disagreement about who should hold power over a potentially transformative technology.
insight: Musk's message is a classic funding-leverage move: withhold capital to force a decision. It works. But Sutskever's reply exposes what the document calls the real problem — that Musk's behavior in the negotiation ('absolute control is extremely important to you') contradicted his stated intent. This is a governance trap. When you design a structure to give yourself override authority 'just in case,' you have already built the dictatorship you claim to fear in others. Sutskever names it plainly: the goal is to 'avoid an AGI dictatorship,' and a structure where any single person — including a founder — can seize control defeats that goal regardless of current intentions. The frame here is principal-agent risk applied inward: the biggest governance threat was not an outside competitor but the founding structure itself.
application: Before your next funding or equity negotiation, write down your stated values about control, then map every structural clause against them. If you find a clause that gives you unilateral override 'only in emergencies,' ask whether a neutral observer would read that as consistent with what you said. If not, fix the clause before the other side names the contradiction for you — because they will.
